Within 30 days after the cutoff, as news spreads about the deaths of soldiers on the attacking side, will there be large-scale anti-war demonstrations in the attacked country, demanding that the new leadership immediately stop counterattack?

Within 60 days after the cutoff, mainstream public opinion will generally praise the attacker's "talk and fight" strategy as "rational restraint" and believe that its ultimatum shows the sincerity of a responsible major country?

time.desc: For the first time, one warring party publicly admitted that its own soldiers were killed in the conflict, saying that the casualties came from the other side's drone attacks on overseas support bases.

The attacked country officially confirmed the completion of the wartime succession of the highest power position. The new supreme leader made an appearance and a loyalty rally occurred in the capital.

The attackers' air strikes hit the islands where the country's key crude oil export hubs are located and surrounding military air defense facilities. The outside world is paying attention to the risks of energy exports.

The leader of the attacking party made provocative statements in public and on social platforms about the life and death of the new supreme leader of the attacked country and his intention to negotiate. The attacked country responded with an open letter and official refutation of the rumors, emphasizing that it was willing to talk but would not surrender.

A senior economic official from the attacking side made a policy statement on the position of navigation in the key strait and the response to the energy market, saying that there is currently no objection to the passage of some ships and that follow-up measures will be linked to the length of the war.

The coalition forces launched a new round of air strikes on energy infrastructure such as the super-large natural gas fields of the affected country, triggering significant fluctuations in international oil prices and accompanied by statements that "the war will be ended as soon as possible"

The leader of the offensive side issued a time-limited ultimatum to the attacked country, demanding that commercial shipping in the key strait be restored, otherwise its critical civilian infrastructure such as power will be hit.

The armed forces of the attacked country responded by saying that if the other party implements the threat of attacking energy facilities, it will completely close the key strait, and the conflict and the threat of sanctions will escalate each other.
The attacker announced that it has opened dialogue with the attacked country and promised to temporarily suspend attacks on its energy facilities to create a limited window for negotiations.
The offensive side formally submitted a multi-clause plan to end the conflict to the attacked country in an attempt to push for a break in the ceasefire negotiations.
The attacked country completed its official response to the attacker's multi-term ceasefire plan. The ceasefire negotiations entered a new stage and the key Strait issue became the core disagreement.

The two countries outside the region jointly proposed a multi-point plan for "immediate ceasefire and restoration of normal traffic in key straits", forming a third-party mediation path that is different from the warring parties' plans.
In a nationally televised address, the leader of the attackers announced a tougher crackdown in the coming weeks and reiterated a timetable for ending the conflict.

The leader of the attacking party publicly threatened to bomb the attacked country's power plants, bridges and other infrastructure. The attacked party warned that it would block another key waterway as a counter-escalation option.

The leaders of the attacking side agreed to suspend bombing of the attacked country for two weeks and triggered a sharp decline in the energy market. The ceasefire window opened but the follow-up direction is unclear.

Leaders of allied countries stated that the ceasefire did not cover their military operations against armed forces of the attacked parties. Third parties urged that the front be included in the ceasefire, triggering controversy over the "loopholes" in the ceasefire.

The attacking military officially launched a naval blockade of the ports of the attacked country and stated that it would not hinder the passage of ports in non-attacked countries. The prospect of a regional ceasefire has once again become uncertain.
The army of the attacked party launched a new round of large-scale counterattack and fired missiles at a warship of the attacking party, while denying that it had closed the key strait.

For the first time, people in the security circles of the attacking side admitted that there was no feasible plan for regime change before the air strike. The focus of the conflict turned to the whereabouts of the highly enriched uranium of the attacked side.
The attacked side confirmed that another core high-level official was killed in the opponent's air strike, becoming one of the highest-level officials to be eliminated since the war began.
The leader of a major country publicly called on all countries on social media to go to key straits to compete for oil resources, claiming that the rival country has been defeated.
The two major powers launched joint air strikes on the petrochemical special economic zone in the southwest of the rival country, hitting its energy industry center and causing injuries.

Rival countries held commemorative events for forty days after the death of their supreme leader. The successor supreme leader gave a speech and continued to argue over disputes such as tolls for passage through the Strait.
The navy of a major country began to blockade the opponent's ports and mobilized troops in key straits, just as the two sides were holding talks on strait issues.
